q: A retailer stores each customer order as a JSON document with a flexible set of fields that can vary from order to order. How should this data best be classified?
why: JSON documents have some organization, like keys and nesting, but no fixed schema shared identically by every record, which is the definition of semi-structured data. Structured and relational data require a fixed schema of rows and columns, and unstructured data, like a plain video file, has no inherent organization at all.

q: An application needs to record thousands of small, fast purchase transactions per second, each affecting only a few rows at a time. Which type of workload is this?
why: OLTP workloads are optimized for many fast, small, individual transactions, like recording a single purchase, matching thousands of small operations per second. OLAP and data warehousing are optimized for large analytical queries over historical data rather than fast individual writes, and batch analytics processes data in scheduled groups rather than transaction by transaction.

q: A data engineering team lands daily sales extracts in a data lake. Analysts typically query two or three columns out of sixty across billions of rows, and storage cost matters. Which file format best fits the curated copy of this data?
why: Parquet is a columnar binary format, so a query touching three of sixty columns reads only those columns, and column-wise compression keeps storage small. Avro is also binary and compressed but row-based, so every row's full width is read; it suits streaming ingestion and schema evolution rather than analytical scans. CSV and JSON Lines are row-oriented text formats with no column pruning and weak compression.

q: A social media application needs to store rapidly changing, loosely structured user activity data at massive global scale, with flexible schemas that evolve often. Which type of database is generally the better fit?
opts: A relational database with a fixed schema
why: A non-relational (NoSQL) database is built for flexible, evolving schemas and massive horizontal scale, matching a social app's loosely structured, high-volume activity data. A relational database assumes a fixed schema, and a data warehouse or OLAP cube is built for structured historical reporting, not rapidly changing operational data.

q: After a failed deployment, a company needs someone to restore last night's Azure SQL Database backup, rebuild fragmented indexes, and tighten which logins can read the Customers table. Which role should own these tasks?
why: Backup and restore, index maintenance, and login permissions are the day-to-day operational care of a database, which is the Database Administrator's remit. A Data Engineer builds the pipelines that move and transform data into and out of that database rather than administering it, a Data Analyst consumes it to build reports, and a Data Scientist uses it to train and evaluate models.

q: A banking application must guarantee that a funds transfer either fully completes, moving money out of one account and into another, or does not happen at all, even if the system crashes mid-transfer. Which property is this describing?
why: Atomicity makes the two updates one indivisible unit: both happen or neither does, which is the all-or-nothing behavior described. Durability would only guarantee that a transfer already committed survives the crash, not that a half-finished one is undone. Isolation keeps concurrent transfers from seeing each other's uncommitted changes, and Consistency ensures the result obeys the database's rules, such as a balance constraint; neither is the all-or-nothing guarantee itself.

q: A dataset arrives continuously from thousands of IoT sensors, in several different formats, at high volume, with some readings of uncertain accuracy. Which big data characteristic specifically refers to the uncertain accuracy of the readings?
why: Veracity refers specifically to the trustworthiness and accuracy of data, which matches readings of uncertain accuracy. Volume refers to the amount of data, velocity to the speed it arrives, and variety to the different formats involved — none of those describe how trustworthy the data is.

q: A team wants to ingest massive amounts of raw data of every type — video, JSON logs, and CSV extracts — without first defining a fixed schema, to be processed and structured later. Which storage concept fits best?
why: A data lake is built to accept massive amounts of raw data of any type, structured or not, without requiring a schema up front. A relational database and a data warehouse both expect data to already be structured and modeled, and an OLAP cube is a pre-aggregated structure built on top of already-modeled data, not a raw ingestion target.

q: Because a data warehouse is loaded from the records of a transactional database, the warehouse itself is still considered an OLTP system.
why: Where the data came from does not define the workload type. A data warehouse serves OLAP: read-heavy, aggregating queries over large volumes of historical data, usually denormalized into a star schema. The source system that recorded each transaction is the OLTP side, optimized for many short, fast reads and writes of individual records.

q: A CSV export in which every row has the same comma-separated columns is semi-structured data, because it is stored as a plain-text file rather than in a database table.
why: Structure is about the data's shape, not its container. A delimited file whose rows all share one fixed set of columns is tabular, so it is structured data even though it lives in a text file. Semi-structured data, such as JSON or XML, has organizing elements like keys and tags but no single schema every record must match.

q: A company is staffing an analytics project. Which of the following tasks would typically be assigned to a Data Engineer? (Choose two.)
opts: Designing the pipeline that copies data from on-premises SQL Server into a data lake each night
Cleansing and transforming the raw files into curated tables ready for analysis
Setting the backup retention period and tuning indexes on the source database
Building the interactive report that business users open each morning
why: Building ingestion pipelines and transforming raw data into curated, analysis-ready form is the core of the Data Engineer role. Backup retention and index tuning on a production database are operational care that belongs to the Database Administrator, and the finished report is the Data Analyst's deliverable, even though both depend on the engineer's pipeline.

q: A customer's payment is confirmed, and one second later the database server loses power. When the server restarts, the payment is still recorded. Which ACID property guarantees this?
why: Durability guarantees that once a transaction is committed its changes survive a crash or power loss, which is exactly what a confirmed payment reappearing after restart demonstrates. Atomicity governs a transaction still in progress, ensuring it fully completes or is fully undone, not the survival of one already committed. Consistency keeps the database within its rules, and Isolation separates concurrent transactions; neither is about surviving a failure.

q: A team is cataloging its data estate. Which of the following would be classified as semi-structured or unstructured data? (Choose two.)
opts: An XML order message whose optional elements vary from order to order
A JPEG photo of each delivered package
A Parquet file with a defined set of typed columns
A table in Azure SQL Database
why: XML with varying optional elements is semi-structured: self-describing tags, but no single schema every message must match. A photo is unstructured, since nothing inside the file is organized into fields. The Parquet file is the near miss: although it is a file in a lake rather than a database row, it carries a fixed set of typed columns, which makes it structured, just like the SQL table.

q: Which of the following tasks would typically be assigned to a Data Analyst rather than another data role? (Choose two.)
opts: Modeling relationships and measures in a Power BI dataset for a sales report
Building and publishing an interactive dashboard for regional managers
Provisioning the Azure SQL Database and configuring its automated backups
Writing the Azure Data Factory pipeline that loads the warehouse nightly
why: Data modeling for reporting and building the dashboards and reports stakeholders use are the Data Analyst's work. Provisioning and configuring backups on the database is the Database Administrator's responsibility, and designing the loading pipeline belongs to the Data Engineer, even though the analyst depends on both.

q: A marketing director asks for an interactive report that lets her slice last quarter's campaign results by region and channel, built on a Power BI data model with calculated measures. Which role is primarily responsible for delivering this?
why: Exploring data, modeling it for reporting, and building interactive visualizations for business stakeholders is the Data Analyst role. A Data Scientist would be the fit if the ask were a predictive model rather than a descriptive report, a Data Engineer builds the pipelines that supply the data, and a Database Administrator maintains the databases those pipelines read from.

q: A relational database enforces a rule that an account balance can never go negative, and rejects any transaction that would violate this rule, always leaving the database in a valid state. Which ACID property does this describe?
why: Consistency guarantees that a transaction only ever moves the database from one valid state to another, enforcing rules like a balance constraint and rejecting anything that would violate it. Atomicity is about a transaction being all-or-nothing, Durability is about committed changes surviving a crash, and Isolation is about concurrent transactions not interfering with each other — none of which describe enforcing a specific business rule like this one.

q: Because a data lake stores raw files in whatever format they arrive, the data in it cannot be queried with SQL until it has been loaded into a data warehouse.
why: A data lake applies schema-on-read, so structure is imposed at query time rather than on the way in. Services such as a Synapse serverless SQL pool, or external tables in a dedicated pool, run SQL directly over files like Parquet and CSV sitting in the lake. Loading into a warehouse is a performance and modeling choice, not a prerequisite for querying.

q: A law firm scans signed paper contracts into image files and stores them with no accompanying metadata. A separate system later extracts clause text from each one into JSON. How should the scanned image files themselves be classified?
why: A scanned image has no internal fields, tags, or schema that a system can interpret, which makes it unstructured data regardless of what text it depicts. The JSON produced afterward is the semi-structured artifact, with keys but no fixed schema; structured data would require a fixed set of columns, and streaming describes how data arrives, not its shape.

q: A retail chain needs a system that can answer 'total sales by region by quarter for the last five years,' aggregating across millions of historical transactions, without slowing down the system processing today's in-store purchases. Which workload type fits the reporting need?
opts: OLTP, running the reports against the normalized order-entry database
OLAP, running the reports against a separate denormalized store
OLTP, with the historical rows archived to a read-only table first
OLAP, running the reports directly inside the point-of-sale database
why: Sweeping aggregations over years of history are an OLAP workload, and keeping them in a separate, denormalized store such as a data warehouse is what stops them from competing with live purchases. Running them against the normalized order-entry database, archived or not, keeps heavy reads on the OLTP system and its join-heavy schema. Calling the work OLAP but running it inside the point-of-sale database still shares the same compute, which is the contention the scenario is trying to avoid.

q: Two bank transfer transactions run at the same time against the same account, and the database ensures neither transaction can see the other's uncommitted, in-progress changes. Which ACID property is this?
why: Isolation is specifically about concurrent transactions not seeing each other's uncommitted changes. Atomicity means a transaction fully completes or fully rolls back, durability means a committed change survives a crash, and consistency means the database only moves between states that satisfy its rules (like a balance never going negative) — a related but distinct guarantee from concurrent visibility.

q: A team is training and evaluating a model that predicts which customers are likely to cancel their subscription next month, using several years of historical usage data. Which role is primarily responsible for this work?
why: A Data Scientist builds, trains, and evaluates predictive models like a churn predictor from historical data. A Database Administrator maintains the databases themselves, a Data Analyst builds descriptive reports rather than predictive models, and a Business Analyst focuses on business requirements rather than model development.

q: Schema-on-read means data is validated against a fixed schema and rejected if it doesn't match, before it is ever written to storage.
why: That describes schema-on-write, the relational database approach. Schema-on-read stores data as-is and applies structure only later, when it's queried — the approach a data lake takes with raw files.

q: A telemetry system stores billions of sparse rows where different rows can have very different sets of populated columns, and needs extremely fast writes at massive scale. Which non-relational data store shape fits best?
why: A column-family store groups sparse, wide sets of columns together and is built for exactly this kind of massive write-scale with varying populated columns per row. A document store models self-contained records with a more uniform internal shape, a key-value store pairs one simple value per key, and a graph store emphasizes relationships between entities rather than sparse wide-column layout.

q: Which of the following are examples of data ingestion? (Choose two.)
opts: Loading nightly export files from an on-premises system into a data lake
Continuously receiving clickstream events from a website into a streaming pipeline
Building a Power BI report on top of data that's already been loaded
Writing documentation describing what each column in a table means
why: Data ingestion is collecting and importing data into a storage or processing system, matching both the nightly file load and the continuous clickstream feed. Building a report consumes data that's already been ingested rather than ingesting it, and writing column documentation is a governance activity, not an ingestion step.

q: A system requires every row inserted into a table to already match a predefined set of columns and data types, rejecting anything that doesn't conform, before it is stored at all. Which concept does this describe?
why: Validating data against a fixed schema at insert time, and rejecting what doesn't fit, is schema-on-write, the relational database approach. Schema-on-read stores data as-is and applies structure at query time. Referential integrity is narrower: it checks that a foreign key points at an existing row, not that every column matches a type. Normalization is a design process for arranging tables, not a check applied to incoming rows.

q: A compliance officer wants to trace a suspicious number appearing in a quarterly report all the way back to the source system and every transformation it passed through along the way. Which concept describes this traceable history?
why: Data lineage is the traceable history of where a piece of data originated and what transformations it passed through on its way to a report, exactly what the compliance officer needs to trace. Data classification labels data by sensitivity rather than tracing its history, data redundancy is about keeping extra copies for durability, and data retention governs how long data is kept, not where it came from.

q: Classifying a dataset as 'Highly Confidential' in Microsoft Purview also determines how many years the data must be kept before it can be deleted.
why: Classification labels data by sensitivity so access and handling rules can follow it consistently; how long data must be kept is governed by a separate retention policy, driven by legal or business requirements. The two often apply to the same dataset, but a sensitivity label says who may see it, not when it may be destroyed.

q: A compliance team is evaluating Microsoft Purview. Which of the following needs would it address? (Choose three.)
opts: Producing a searchable catalog of every data store across several subscriptions
Flagging columns that appear to contain national ID numbers and labeling them as sensitive
Showing which upstream tables and pipelines a report's figures were derived from
Encrypting an Azure SQL database's files at rest so stolen storage is unreadable
why: Discovery and cataloging, automatic classification with sensitivity labels, and lineage tracking are Purview's core governance capabilities. Encryption at rest is the near miss: it is a protection the database engine itself provides through Transparent Data Encryption, which Purview can report on but does not perform.

q: A healthcare organization must keep patient billing records for seven years before they can be deleted, driven by a legal requirement rather than a storage cost decision. Which concept describes this seven-year rule itself?
why: The rule stating how long a category of data must be kept, and why, is a data retention policy. A lifecycle management rule is the closest alternative, but it is the storage-level mechanism that would carry the policy out by tiering or deleting blobs on a schedule, not the requirement itself. A classification label describes sensitivity, and a lineage record describes where data came from, not how long it must survive.

q: A data engineering team stores analytics tables as files in a data lake and needs ACID transactions, data versioning, and reliable updates on top of those files, without moving to a separate database engine. Which format adds these capabilities to Parquet files?
why: Delta Lake is an open-source storage format that builds on Parquet by adding a transaction log, which enables ACID transactions, versioning, and reliable updates. Avro is a row-based format with a JSON header describing binary records, but it has no transaction layer. CSV and XML are human-readable text formats with neither transactions nor versioning.

q: A team streams events between systems and wants a compact, row-based binary format in which each file starts with a header, stored as JSON, that describes the structure of the records. Which format fits?
why: Avro is a row-based format whose header, stored as JSON, describes the binary records that follow, and it is good at minimizing storage and network bandwidth. Parquet is the near miss: it is binary but columnar, built for reading selected columns in analytics. CSV and XML are human-readable text formats rather than compact binary ones.

q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between document databases and key-value databases?
opts: A document database is a specific form of key-value database in which the value is a JSON document that the system is optimized to parse and query
A document database stores only relational tables whose rows are linked by foreign keys
A key-value database always requires its values to be stored as JSON documents
A document database is the same thing as a graph database that models nodes and edges
why: In a key-value database each record has a unique key and a value in any format. A document database narrows that to JSON documents that the system can parse and query. Document databases do not use relational tables, key-value values are not required to be JSON, and graph databases are a different model built around nodes and edges.

q: A company stores customers' scanned photos and videos, billing records that need joins across many tables, and a social graph of friendships. Which assignment of stores is the best fit for these three kinds of data in order?
opts: Azure SQL Database, Blob Storage, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
Blob Storage, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin, Azure SQL Database
Blob Storage, Azure SQL Database, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
Azure Files, Azure Table Storage, Azure SQL Database
why: Photos and videos are unstructured binary objects, which Blob Storage handles. Billing records needing joins across many tables suit a relational database such as Azure SQL Database, and a social graph where relationships matter as much as the entities suits the Gremlin graph API of Cosmos DB. The other orders put relational joins on Blob Storage or graph data on a relational or key-value store.

q: XML has largely replaced JSON as the preferred format for modern web APIs because it is less verbose.
why: It is the other way around. XML is human-readable and tag-based, was popular in the 1990s and 2000s, and has largely been superseded by the less verbose JSON, although some systems still use it.

q: Which two pairings of workload and Azure data store are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A mountable shared file share replacing an on-premises file server: Azure Files
Highly connected social-network relationships: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
Complex multi-table joins with strict relationships: Azure Cosmos DB
A raw archive of video files: Azure SQL Database
why: Azure Files provides mountable file shares and the Gremlin API models relationship-heavy graph data. Complex multi-table joins belong in a relational engine such as Azure SQL Database, and video files are unstructured objects that belong in Blob Storage rather than a relational database.

q: A database designer is reviewing the keys on an Orders table that references a Customers table. Which of the following statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: A table can have only one primary key, although that key may span several columns
Each foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table, or be null
A foreign key column must hold a unique value in every row of its own table
A primary key column may contain nulls as long as the remaining rows stay distinct
why: A table has exactly one primary key, which can be composite, and a foreign key either points at an existing row in the referenced table or is null; that is referential integrity. The near miss is uniqueness: a foreign key such as CustomerID repeats on every order that customer places, so it is not unique within Orders. A primary key, by contrast, can never be null, because a null cannot identify a row.

q: A Customers table and an Orders table are related so that every order must reference a valid, existing customer. Which concept enforces this rule?
opts: Normalization applied to both tables to remove any repeating groups
A foreign key referencing the Customers table
A primary key defined on the Orders table's own order ID column
A data warehouse star schema linking Orders to a Customer dimension
why: A foreign key in the Orders table that references the Customers table's primary key is exactly the mechanism that enforces every order pointing to a valid customer. Normalization is the broader design process, a primary key on Orders only identifies order rows themselves without referencing another table, and a star schema is a data warehouse modeling pattern, not a relational integrity rule.

q: Splitting a single large table that repeats customer address details on every order row into two related tables, Orders and Customers, is an example of which process?
why: Splitting repeated data into separate related tables to reduce redundancy is the definition of normalization. Denormalization does the opposite — deliberately reintroducing redundancy for read performance — while sharding and partitioning are about distributing data across physical storage, not about eliminating redundant columns.

q: A company is migrating an on-premises SQL Server database that relies on cross-database queries and SQL Server Agent jobs, and wants the least re-engineering while still moving to a managed Azure service. Which option fits best?
why: Azure SQL Managed Instance offers near-complete SQL Server compatibility, including cross-database queries and SQL Server Agent, making it the best fit for a lift-and-shift with minimal re-engineering. Azure SQL Database does not support cross-database queries or SQL Agent the same way, and Table Storage and Cosmos DB are non-relational services entirely.

q: A team needs full administrative control over the operating system hosting their SQL Server instance, including installing custom OS-level software alongside it. Which deployment option fits?
opts: SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine
why: SQL Server on an Azure VM is an IaaS option, giving full administrative control over the operating system, including installing arbitrary OS-level software. Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance are both PaaS, where Microsoft manages the OS, and Azure Database for MySQL is a different database engine entirely.

q: A company already runs its application on open-source PostgreSQL and wants a fully managed Azure equivalent without switching database engines. Which service fits?
why: Azure Database for PostgreSQL is the managed PaaS offering for the PostgreSQL engine itself, so the application keeps its existing driver, SQL dialect, and extensions. Azure Database for MySQL is also managed open source, but it is a different engine with a different dialect, so it would still be a migration. Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance both run the SQL Server engine, which the company has said it does not want to switch to.

q: A company already owns SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance and wants to apply them to reduce its Azure SQL Database bill. It also wants to add compute during month-end without changing storage size. Which purchasing model should it choose?
why: Only the vCore model supports Azure Hybrid Benefit, which is what lets existing licenses offset the cost, and it prices compute and storage separately so one can be scaled without the other. The DTU model bundles compute, memory, and storage into a single blended unit and cannot apply the license benefit; an eDTU pool is simply the DTU model shared across databases, and Basic is the smallest DTU tier, so both inherit the same limitations.

q: A read-heavy reporting database joins six normalized tables for almost every query, and response times are slow. The team is willing to store some duplicated data in exchange for faster reads. What should they do?
opts: Denormalize the schema by combining the most frequently joined tables
Normalize the schema further to remove any remaining redundancy
Add a foreign key constraint between each pair of joined tables
Shard the six tables across several separate databases
why: Denormalization deliberately reintroduces redundancy so a query can read one wide table instead of joining six, which is the trade the team has said it will accept. Further normalization moves in the opposite direction and adds joins. Foreign key constraints enforce integrity but do not make joins cheaper. Sharding distributes rows across databases for scale, and would make joins across those tables harder, not faster.

q: An application that depends on SQL Server Agent jobs can be moved to Azure SQL Database without changes, because every PaaS SQL offering in Azure includes SQL Server Agent.
why: SQL Server Agent is an instance-level feature that Azure SQL Database does not provide; its jobs would need to be re-implemented with Elastic Jobs, Azure Automation, or a similar service. Azure SQL Managed Instance is the PaaS option that keeps SQL Server Agent, along with cross-database queries and other instance-scoped features, which is exactly why it exists for lift-and-shift migrations.

q: A company has just deployed Azure SQL Database and is documenting which operational tasks its own staff must still perform. Which task remains the customer's responsibility?
opts: Creating indexes and tuning queries for the application's workload
Applying security patches to the SQL Server database engine
why: In a PaaS database Microsoft patches the engine and operating system and maintains the hardware, but the customer still owns the schema, indexing, and query design, because only they know the application's workload. The other three tasks are precisely what moves to Microsoft when choosing Azure SQL Database over SQL Server on a virtual machine, where OS patching would still fall to the customer.

q: A team is comparing SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine with Azure SQL Managed Instance. Which responsibilities belong to the customer with the VM option but not with Managed Instance? (Choose two.)
opts: Designing the database schema and indexes
why: SQL Server on a VM is IaaS: the customer patches the operating system and updates the SQL Server software, both of which Microsoft handles in Managed Instance. Physical hardware is Microsoft's responsibility in both cases, since even a VM runs on Azure infrastructure, and schema and index design remain the customer's job in both, because no service model takes over application design.

q: A company wants to host a relational workload in Azure and insists that Microsoft, not its own staff, patches the database engine. Which deployment options satisfy this? (Choose three.)
opts: SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine
why: Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL are all managed PaaS relational services in which Microsoft patches the engine and operating system. SQL Server on a VM is relational but IaaS, so the customer applies SQL Server and OS updates themselves. Cosmos DB for NoSQL is fully managed, but it is a non-relational document store, so it fails the relational requirement.

q: Queries that filter the Orders table by CustomerEmail have become slow as the table has grown to millions of rows, while inserts are still fast. Which change most directly speeds up those filtered reads?
opts: Creating an index on the CustomerEmail column
Creating a view that selects from the Orders table
Moving the query into a stored procedure
Adding a foreign key from Orders to Customers
why: An index on CustomerEmail lets the engine seek directly to matching rows instead of scanning millions, at the cost of a little extra storage and slightly slower writes. A view only saves a query definition and runs the same scan underneath; a stored procedure packages logic on the server but does not change how rows are located; and a foreign key enforces referential integrity rather than accelerating a filter on a non-key column.

q: A company runs 50 small Azure SQL databases with unpredictable usage that rarely peaks for every database at the same time. Provisioning each database for its own worst case would be expensive. Which deployment option lets these databases share a pool of resources to reduce cost?
opts: An elastic pool sharing resources across many databases
SQL Server on an Azure Virtual Machine, managed as 50 separate instances
A single database sized for its own individual peak load, repeated for each of the 50
Read scale-out replicas added to each database individually
why: An elastic pool lets many databases with staggered, non-simultaneous usage share one billed pool of resources instead of each being sized for its own peak, matching this cost-saving scenario. SQL Server on a VM adds unrelated OS management overhead on top of the same per-database sizing problem, sizing every database for its own peak is the expensive approach being avoided, and read scale-out only offloads read queries to a replica rather than pooling compute across many databases.

q: The high availability built into every Azure SQL Database also keeps the database available through the loss of an entire Azure region, with no additional configuration.
why: Built-in high availability protects against node and, when zone redundancy is enabled, datacenter failures within one region. Surviving the loss of the whole region requires a readable secondary elsewhere, which means configuring active geo-replication or a failover group; those are opt-in business continuity features, not part of the default deployment.

q: A table's Employees.ManagerID column stores the EmployeeID of that employee's manager, who is also just another row in the same Employees table. What kind of relationship does this represent?
opts: A many-to-many relationship requiring a junction table
why: A foreign key column referencing the primary key of the very same table is a self-referencing, or recursive, relationship — common for modeling hierarchies like org charts. There's no separate junction table involved since each employee has just one manager, this isn't a data warehouse fact/dimension pattern, and it's a relational foreign key, not a non-relational document reference.

q: An application's Azure SQL Database is approaching 4 TB and is expected to keep growing well past that, with an occasional need for near-instant storage scaling and fast database restores regardless of size. Which service tier fits best?
opts: The Basic tier with manual sharding
why: Hyperscale supports databases up to 128 TB with rapid storage scaling and restore times that stay fast regardless of database size, matching both stated needs. Standard and General Purpose both have much lower practical size ceilings and restore times that grow with database size, and the Basic tier is meant for small, light workloads, not multi-terabyte growth.

q: An elastic pool is the ideal choice when all of its databases reach peak load at the same hour each day, because the pool guarantees each database its own dedicated peak capacity.
why: An elastic pool shares one allocation of compute among its databases, so it saves money precisely when their peaks are staggered and the pool can be sized well below the sum of the individual peaks. If every database spikes simultaneously, they all compete for the same pooled resources and the pool must be sized for the combined peak, erasing the saving; individually provisioned databases would fit that pattern better.

q: A team's Azure SQL Database has grown to multiple terabytes, and heavy reporting queries are starting to compete with the production application for the same compute. The team wants to offload those reporting queries to a dedicated read-only replica without duplicating the whole database into a separate service. Which service tier offers this kind of built-in read-scale replica?
why: Hyperscale supports built-in read-scale replicas that let reporting queries run against a separate compute replica without competing with the primary or duplicating the database into a whole separate service. Standard and General Purpose don't offer this same built-in multi-replica read-scale capability, and the Basic tier is meant for small, lightweight workloads, not multi-terabyte databases needing replica offload.

q: A company needs its Azure SQL Database connections to automatically redirect to a readable secondary database in another region during a regional outage, without the application needing to track which region is currently active. Which capability provides this?
why: A failover group layers a stable listener endpoint on top of geo-replication, so the application keeps one connection string and is redirected automatically when failover occurs. Active geo-replication alone creates the readable secondary but leaves the application to switch connection strings itself. Zone-redundant configuration spreads replicas across availability zones inside one region and does not survive a regional outage, and an elastic pool shares compute among databases in a single region.

q: An operations team is listing the business continuity protections an Azure SQL Database offers. Which of the following are correct? (Choose three.)
opts: Automated backups allow point-in-time restore to a moment within the retention period
Active geo-replication maintains readable secondary databases in other regions
A failover group provides a single connection endpoint that follows the primary after failover
Automated backups are retained indefinitely at no additional cost
why: Point-in-time restore from automated backups, readable geo-secondaries, and the failover group's stable endpoint are all genuine capabilities. The near miss is retention: automated backups are kept for a configurable short-term window, and keeping them longer requires a long-term retention policy that is charged for separately, so 'indefinitely at no cost' is wrong.

q: An audit requires that an Azure SQL Database's data files and backups be unreadable if the underlying storage were ever stolen. Application queries must not change, and authorized DBAs must still be able to see the actual column values. Which feature meets this?
why: Transparent Data Encryption encrypts the database files, logs, and backups at rest, is invisible to queries, and decrypts data for any authenticated user, so DBAs still see real values. Always Encrypted is the near miss: it protects data at rest too, but it keeps values encrypted even from DBAs and requires client-side driver changes. Dynamic Data Masking only alters query results for some users, and row-level security filters which rows a user can see; neither protects stolen storage.

q: A support team needs to query a customer table to troubleshoot issues, but should see only the last four digits of each customer's credit card number rather than the full value, without the underlying stored data ever changing. Which feature fits?
opts: Denying SELECT permission on the card number column
why: Dynamic Data Masking rewrites the values returned to non-privileged users, for example showing XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-1234, while the stored data and privileged users' results are untouched. Transparent Data Encryption protects files at rest and returns full values to anyone who can query. Row-level security hides entire rows rather than part of a column. Denying SELECT on the column blocks the support team from seeing it at all, including the last four digits they need.

q: An internal expense application uses Azure SQL Database only during business hours, sits idle overnight and on weekends, and has light, unpredictable load. The team wants the lowest cost without managing capacity by hand. Which option fits best?
opts: The serverless compute tier in the General Purpose service tier
Provisioned compute in the Business Critical service tier
The Hyperscale service tier with one secondary replica
An elastic pool containing only this database
why: Serverless compute scales vCores up and down with demand, bills per second of use, and can auto-pause during the long idle stretches so only storage is charged. Business Critical provisions premium compute around the clock whether or not anyone is using it. Hyperscale targets very large or fast-growing databases, not a small intermittent one. An elastic pool only pays off when several databases share it; a pool for a single database just adds a provisioned reservation.

q: A security review asks which Azure SQL Database features limit what sensitive data an attacker or an over-privileged user could read. Which of the following qualify? (Choose two.)
opts: Transparent Data Encryption, which encrypts data files and backups at rest
Dynamic Data Masking, which obscures column values returned to non-privileged users
Point-in-time restore, which recovers the database to an earlier moment
Active geo-replication, which keeps a readable copy in another region
why: Transparent Data Encryption protects the data if storage or backups are stolen, and Dynamic Data Masking limits what low-privilege accounts see in query results, so both reduce exposure of sensitive data. Point-in-time restore and geo-replication are business continuity features: they protect against data loss and outages, but a restored or replicated copy exposes exactly the same data as the original.

q: Before migrating an on-premises SQL Server database to Azure, a team wants a tool that analyzes their databases and reports compatibility issues that could block the move to Azure SQL Managed Instance or Azure SQL Database. Which tool fits?
why: Data Migration Assistant analyzes SQL Server databases and reports issues that could block migration, such as features a target does not support (Microsoft retired the tool on July 16, 2025, but DP-900 material still names it for this job). Data Factory and SQL Server Integration Services move and transform data but do not assess compatibility, and Purview catalogs and classifies data rather than checking migration readiness.

q: A team is starting a new MySQL-based workload on Azure and wants granular control over configuration and management settings, plus cost optimization controls, in a fully managed service. Which deployment option does Microsoft recommend for new MySQL workloads?
opts: Azure SQL Managed Instance with an instance pool
Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server
why: The flexible-server deployment option for Azure Database for MySQL is fully managed, gives more granular control over configuration and cost, and is the recommended option for new workloads. Managed Instance and SQL Server on a VM are SQL Server products rather than MySQL, and Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra is a NoSQL column-family API.

q: A script runs CREATE INDEX on the Orders table, then INSERT adds new orders, then GRANT lets an analyst role read the table. In order, which SQL statement categories do these three statements belong to?
why: CREATE INDEX changes structure, so it is data definition language, INSERT works with rows, so it is data manipulation language, and GRANT manages permissions, so it is data control language. The other orders swap categories: INSERT is not DDL or DCL, and GRANT is not DML.

q: A DBA wants analysts to query the result of a join across three tables as if it were a single table, exposing only selected columns, without copying the data anywhere. Which database object fits?
why: A view is a saved query that presents the result, such as a join and chosen columns, as a virtual table without storing a separate copy of the data. An index speeds up lookups on a table, a stored procedure is a named, reusable routine you call explicitly, and a trigger runs automatically when a data change event occurs.

q: Whenever a row in the Orders table is deleted, the database must automatically write a record to an audit table, without the application having to ask for it. Which object does this?
why: A trigger is a routine that fires automatically in response to an event such as an insert, update, or delete. A view only presents data, a foreign key constraint enforces valid relationships rather than performing an action, and an index speeds lookups.

q: A database trigger runs only when an application explicitly calls it by name, in the same way as a stored procedure.
why: A stored procedure is called explicitly, usually with parameters. A trigger fires automatically when a defined event, such as an insert, update, or delete, occurs.

q: Which two capabilities are described as built into Azure SQL Database? (Choose two.)
opts: Advanced threat protection that includes vulnerability assessments and anomalous-activity detection
Auditing that writes database events to an Azure storage account
Automatic conversion of tables into Cosmos DB containers
A guarantee that no data can ever be lost across regions without any configuration
why: Threat protection and auditing are both described as built-in security and compliance features. Tables are not converted to Cosmos DB containers, and cross-region protection depends on configuring geo-replication or failover groups rather than being automatic and absolute.

q: An application needs a database that can replicate data across multiple regions worldwide with low-latency reads and writes and configurable consistency levels. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
why: Azure Cosmos DB is purpose-built for global distribution with low-latency reads and writes and configurable consistency levels. Azure SQL Database and Table Storage are not designed for turnkey multi-region global distribution in the same way, and Azure Files is a managed file share service, not a globally distributed database.

q: A development team already builds their application using MongoDB drivers and wants to move to a managed Azure database without rewriting their data access code. Which Cosmos DB API fits?
why: The API for MongoDB lets an application built against MongoDB drivers connect to Cosmos DB with minimal code changes. The API for NoSQL (formerly the Core (SQL) API) uses Cosmos DB's native document model instead, the API for Apache Gremlin is for graph data, and the API for Table is for simple key-value data — none of those preserve existing MongoDB driver code.

q: A company needs to store millions of large video files as objects that applications can retrieve over HTTP, with tiers to reduce cost for rarely accessed files. Which service fits best?
why: Azure Blob Storage is object storage designed for large unstructured files like video, accessible over HTTP, with access tiers to reduce cost for infrequently accessed data. Table Storage holds simple structured key-value entities rather than large binary objects, Azure SQL Database is relational, and Cosmos DB is a broader NoSQL database service, not primarily an object store.

q: A big data analytics workload needs an Azure Blob Storage account organized with real directories and folders, plus fine-grained permissions on those folders, for efficient large-scale analytics. Which capability enables this?
opts: Setting the Archive access tier so infrequently touched analytics files cost less to store
Enabling read-access geo-redundant storage so a secondary region can also serve the data
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (hierarchical namespace)
Switching to Azure Table Storage, which already organizes data into folder-like partitions
why: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 adds a hierarchical namespace of real directories and folders with fine-grained permissions on top of Blob Storage, purpose-built for large-scale analytics. The Archive tier and RA-GRS are cost and redundancy settings, not a namespace structure, and Table Storage organizes data by partition key and row key, not real folders — it's an entirely separate, non-hierarchical key-value store.

q: Which of these is the best example of a use case suited to a NoSQL document database rather than a relational database?
opts: Enforcing strict referential integrity between financial ledger transactions
Running complex multi-table joins across normalized tables
Guaranteeing full ACID compliance across multiple related tables
Storing product catalog items where each product has a different, evolving set of attributes
why: A document database handles a catalog where each product can have a different, evolving set of attributes far more naturally than a rigid relational schema would. Referential integrity, complex joins, and full ACID compliance across related tables are all strengths of relational databases, not typical reasons to choose a NoSQL document store.

q: A company wants to fully replace an aging on-premises file server with a cloud equivalent that can still be mounted using the standard SMB protocol from multiple machines. Which service fits?
why: Azure Files provides fully managed file shares accessible over the standard SMB protocol, letting it act as a drop-in replacement for an on-premises file server mounted by multiple machines. Blob Storage and Cosmos DB are not mounted as traditional file shares, and Table Storage holds structured entities, not files.

q: Because Azure Cosmos DB exposes several APIs over one engine, a team can create an account with the Table API, load data, and later switch that same account to the API for MongoDB without migrating the data.
why: The API is chosen when the Cosmos DB account is created and is fixed for that account's lifetime; the APIs share the underlying distributed engine, but each stores and exposes data in its own model. Moving from the Table API to the API for MongoDB means creating a second account and migrating the data, which is why picking the API that matches the application's drivers up front matters.

q: Azure Table Storage can enforce a foreign-key relationship between two of its tables, provided both tables live in the same storage account.
why: Table Storage is a schemaless key-value store: each entity is located by partition key and row key, entities in the same table can have different properties, and there are no joins, foreign keys, or referential integrity across tables. Enforcing that one record must reference a valid record in another table is a relational database feature, such as in Azure SQL Database.

q: A startup wants to avoid relational schema migrations entirely and store records whose fields change from one item to the next. Which Azure services would let it store data without defining a table schema up front? (Choose three.)
why: Cosmos DB for NoSQL stores JSON documents with no fixed schema, Table Storage lets entities in one table carry different properties, and Blob Storage holds any file with no schema at all, so all three are non-relational fits. Azure Database for MySQL and Azure SQL Database are relational engines that require columns and types to be defined before rows are inserted, so each new field would be a schema change.

q: A Cosmos DB container with provisioned throughput costs more than expected, and the team wants to lower the Request Units consumed without changing the data itself. Which change most directly reduces RU consumption per operation?
opts: Replacing cross-partition queries with point reads by id and partition key
Switching the account from the API for NoSQL to the API for Table
Combining several small items into one larger document
Raising the default consistency level to Strong
why: A point read of one item by its id and partition key is the cheapest operation Cosmos DB offers, while a query that fans out across partitions scans and charges for far more. The other options move the wrong way: switching APIs leaves the operation cost unchanged, larger items cost more RUs per read and write because the charge scales with item size, and Strong consistency roughly doubles the RU cost of reads compared with Session.

q: Which of the following are true about Azure Blob Storage access tiers? (Choose three.)
opts: Archive offers the lowest storage cost but blobs must be rehydrated before they can be read
Hot is intended for frequently accessed data and has the lowest per-access cost
Cool trades a lower storage price than Hot for higher access costs
Blobs in the Cool tier must be rehydrated to Hot before an application can read them
why: Archive is offline storage: cheapest to keep, but a blob must be rehydrated, which can take hours, before it is readable. Hot optimizes for access and Cool for storage price, each at the other's expense. The near miss is the claim that Cool blobs need rehydration: Cool and Cold blobs stay online and can be read immediately, just at a higher per-operation charge; only Archive requires rehydration.

q: Which Cosmos DB API would you choose to model and query highly connected data, like a social network's friend-of-a-friend relationships?
why: The API for Apache Gremlin (often called the Gremlin API) is Cosmos DB's graph engine, purpose-built for modeling entities and the relationships between them, like a social graph. The API for Table handles simple key-value data, the API for MongoDB targets document workloads built on MongoDB drivers, and the API for NoSQL (formerly Core (SQL)) is Cosmos DB's native document model — none of the other three is optimized for traversing relationships the way a graph database is.

q: An application currently uses Azure Table Storage for simple key-value data but now needs richer querying, automatic indexing of every property, and global distribution with low-latency reads close to users worldwide. Which service should it move to?
opts: A larger Azure Table Storage account
why: Cosmos DB automatically indexes every property, supports rich querying, and offers global distribution with low-latency reads in each region — everything this scenario needs beyond what Table Storage offers. Blob Storage and Files are built for unstructured objects and file shares respectively rather than queryable records, and simply growing the existing Table Storage account doesn't add global distribution or automatic indexing.

q: A globally distributed Cosmos DB container storing millions of IoT device readings needs its data and throughput spread evenly across many physical partitions, based on a property with many distinct values shared roughly evenly across items. Which setting determines how that data is distributed?
why: The partition key is the item property Cosmos DB hashes to decide which physical partition stores each item, so a key with many evenly used values, such as device id, is what spreads data and load. The indexing policy controls which properties are indexed for queries, not where items live. The consistency level governs how current reads are across replicas, and the throughput mode decides whether RU/s are fixed or autoscaled; neither places data.

q: A web application needs sub-millisecond lookups of each user's session state by session id. The data can be discarded when the session ends and is read thousands of times per second. Which store fits best?
opts: Azure Blob Storage in the Hot tier
why: Session state is small, short-lived, and read constantly, which is the in-memory caching pattern Azure Cache for Redis is built for, with sub-millisecond key lookups. Table Storage is also a cheap key-value store, but it is disk-based and typically responds in milliseconds, not sub-millisecond. Cosmos DB adds durability, global distribution, and RU-based cost the scenario does not need, and Blob Storage is object storage for files rather than a key-value lookup service. (Azure Cache for Redis is being retired in favor of Azure Managed Redis, but the in-memory caching pattern is unchanged.)

q: A Cosmos DB workload has an unpredictable traffic pattern that spikes during promotions and drops the rest of the time, and the team wants throughput to adjust automatically within a set range rather than manually reprovisioning Request Units every time. Which capability fits?
opts: Manual provisioned throughput sized for the peak
why: Autoscale provisioned throughput scales RU/s between ten percent and a maximum the team sets, so capacity follows demand within a known ceiling and the bill tracks actual peaks. Serverless is the near miss: it also avoids manual provisioning, but it has no configurable range and is meant for intermittent, low-traffic workloads rather than a steady baseline with large spikes. Manual throughput sized for the peak pays for the spike all month, and multi-region writes change where writes land, not how much throughput is available.

q: An application needs its Blob Storage data to survive the complete loss of an entire Azure region, and also needs to be able to read that data from the secondary region if the primary region becomes unavailable. Which redundancy option fits?
why: RA-GRS replicates data to a second, distant region and allows read access to that secondary copy, covering both a full regional outage and the ability to keep reading data during one. LRS only protects against hardware failure within a single datacenter, ZRS spreads copies across zones in one region but not to another region, and plain GRS replicates to a second region but doesn't allow reading from it unless a failover occurs.

q: An order-processing application needs to trigger a shipping notification function the moment a new order document is inserted into a Cosmos DB container, without repeatedly polling the container to check for new documents. Which Cosmos DB capability fits?
why: The change feed is a persistent, ordered log of inserts and updates that downstream functions can subscribe to, reacting to changes as they happen instead of polling. A consistency level controls how up to date replicas are, a partition key range affects data distribution, and autoscale throughput adjusts provisioned RU/s — none of those provide a stream of change events to react to.

q: A globally distributed gaming application wants players in both North America and Europe to write their scores to the nearest region with low latency, with both regions accepting writes at the same time rather than every write traveling to one primary region first. Which Cosmos DB capability enables this?
opts: Adding Europe as a read region
Setting the consistency level to Strong
why: Multi-region writes make every configured region writable, so each player's score is committed locally and replicated to the others. Adding Europe as a read region is the near miss: European players would read locally but their writes would still cross the Atlantic to the single write region. Strong consistency makes reads more current at the cost of latency and does not add write regions, and autoscale adjusts RU/s rather than where writes are accepted.

q: Invoices stored as blobs are read often for 30 days, rarely for the following year, and must be kept for seven years in total. The company wants the lowest storage cost with the least ongoing administration. What should it do?
opts: Create a lifecycle management policy that tiers blobs to Cool after 30 days, Archive after a year, and deletes them after seven years
Schedule an Azure Data Factory pipeline that copies aging blobs between storage accounts set to different default tiers
Set the storage account's default access tier to Archive so every invoice is stored at the lowest price
Enable soft delete on the container with a seven-year retention period
why: A lifecycle management policy applies rule-based tiering and deletion automatically based on blob age, which matches the three-stage pattern with no ongoing work. A Data Factory pipeline could move blobs, but it is custom orchestration to maintain for something the storage service does natively. Defaulting everything to Archive would make the first 30 days of frequent reads slow and expensive, since Archive blobs must be rehydrated. Soft delete only protects against accidental deletion; it neither tiers nor expires data.

q: In a data lake organized using the medallion architecture, which of the following correctly describe its zones? (Choose three.)
opts: The bronze zone holds raw data in the form it was ingested, including duplicates and errors
The silver zone holds data that has been cleaned, deduplicated, and validated
The gold zone holds business-ready data modeled for reporting, such as star-schema tables
The silver zone is where finished star-schema tables for Power BI reports are kept
why: Bronze is raw as-landed data, silver is cleaned and conformed, and gold is the refined, business-modeled layer that reports consume. The near miss is the claim that finished star-schema tables live in silver: it describes gold's job and attributes it to silver. Silver data is trustworthy but still shaped like the source systems; the aggregation and dimensional modeling for reporting happen in gold.

q: A shopping app needs each user to always read their own most recent writes within their session, while keeping latency low across a globally distributed Cosmos DB account. Which consistency level is the most widely used and the recommended starting point for most transactional applications?
why: Session consistency guarantees consistency within a single client session, so a user always sees their own writes, and it is the most widely used level and the recommended starting point. Strong gives every reader the latest write everywhere but at the cost of latency, consistent prefix prevents out-of-order reads but can be stale, and eventual is the weakest guarantee.

q: A team wants a Cosmos DB account that is billed only for the Request Units its operations consume and also replicates data to three Azure regions. What is the problem with this plan?
opts: Cosmos DB cannot replicate data to more than one region under any capacity mode
Serverless accounts are limited to a single Azure region, so global distribution needs provisioned throughput
Serverless accounts require a minimum of ten containers before regions can be added
Request Units are only used as a throughput measure with the Table API
why: A serverless account is limited to one region, so replicating to three regions requires a provisioned throughput account, optionally with autoscale. Cosmos DB does replicate across regions, serverless has no container minimum, and Request Units are the throughput currency for all APIs.

q: A container uses country as its partition key, but about 95 percent of the items belong to a single country. Cosmos DB limits a logical partition to 20 GB. What is the best fix?
opts: Convert the container to use the Table API instead of the NoSQL API
Lower the account consistency level to Eventual to relax the size limit
Create a second account in another region and split the traffic
Switch to a property with many distinct, evenly used values, such as a customer or device identifier
why: A good partition key has many distinct values and an even spread of data, so storage and throughput spread across partitions instead of concentrating on one hot, size-limited logical partition. Consistency level, extra regions, and the choice of API do not change how data is distributed across partitions.

q: A new application needs key-value storage at scale with global distribution and automatic secondary indexes, but the developers already know the Azure Table Storage programming model and want minimal code changes. What should they choose?
opts: Azure Table Storage with a larger account
Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
why: Cosmos DB for Table uses the same programming model as Table Storage while adding greater scalability, global distribution, automatic secondary indexes, and instant autoscale, and Microsoft recommends it for new key-value workloads at scale. Table Storage remains supported but has none of those extras, Gremlin is for graph data, and Azure Files is a file share.

q: A company is migrating an existing Apache Cassandra workload that uses the Cassandra Query Language (CQL) and wants a fully managed Azure service with minimal application changes. Which Cosmos DB API fits?
why: Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra is compatible with Cassandra, uses CQL over column-family tables, and suits teams migrating a Cassandra workload. The MongoDB API targets MongoDB applications, the Table API follows the Table Storage key-value model, and the NoSQL API is the native JSON document API with a SQL-like query language.

q: A team plans to mount an NFS Azure file share on its Linux virtual machines. Which statement about NFS Azure file shares is correct?
opts: They require no virtual network because access to the share is always public
They work on HDD-tier accounts and are supported from Windows and macOS clients too
They require an SSD-tier storage account and a virtual network that controls access, and are for Linux clients
They are only available when the share is accessed through Azure File Sync
why: To create an NFS share you must use an SSD-tier storage account and create and configure a virtual network that controls access, and NFS shares are for Linux, not Windows or macOS. SMB is the protocol that works across Windows, Linux, and macOS. NFS shares are not limited to Azure File Sync.

q: A team upgrades an existing storage account to support a hierarchical namespace so it can be used for big-data analytics with folder-level permissions. Which statement is accurate?
opts: The upgrade can be undone at any time from the portal
The upgrade is one-way, and the account cannot be reverted to a flat namespace
Folder-level permissions require Azure SQL Database
The hierarchical namespace removes the account's blob capabilities
why: Enabling the hierarchical namespace, whether at creation or by upgrading, turns the account into Data Lake Storage Gen2 capable storage, and upgrading is a one-way process. It also enables POSIX-style access control lists on files and folders. It does not remove blob capabilities, because Data Lake Storage Gen2 is built on Blob Storage.

q: Microsoft is retiring the Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers of Azure Cache for Redis on September 30, 2028. Which service does Microsoft recommend moving those instances to?
why: Azure Managed Redis is the successor Microsoft recommends for Azure Cache for Redis instances. Table Storage and Cosmos DB for Table are durable key-value stores rather than in-memory caches, and Azure Files is a file share service.

q: Which workload is the poorest fit for Azure Cosmos DB, according to Microsoft's guidance?
opts: Ingesting high-frequency IoT device telemetry from many sensors
An application whose logic depends on complex joins across many related tables
Player profiles and leaderboards for a global online game
A product catalog for a busy e-commerce site
why: Workloads that depend on complex multi-table joins are better suited to a relational database such as Azure SQL Database. Telemetry ingestion, gaming profiles, and retail catalogs are listed as strong fits, because they benefit from a flexible schema, global reach, and low latency.

q: An Azure Cosmos DB serverless account can replicate its data to multiple Azure regions.
why: Serverless accounts are limited to a single Azure region. Applications that need global distribution across multiple regions should use a provisioned throughput account instead, optionally with autoscale.

q: Azure Table Storage has been retired, so existing applications must move to Azure Cosmos DB for Table immediately.
why: Azure Table Storage is still available and supported. Cosmos DB for Table is simply the recommended choice for new workloads that need key-value storage at scale, with greater scalability, global distribution, and automatic secondary indexes.

q: Which three statements about Azure Cosmos DB are correct? (Choose three.)
opts: It automatically indexes all item properties by default
A logical partition can hold up to 20 GB of data
Throughput can be shared at the database level across up to 25 containers
Serverless accounts support global distribution across many regions
why: Cosmos DB indexes every property by default, limits a logical partition to 20 GB, and allows shared throughput across up to 25 containers. Serverless accounts are limited to a single Azure region, so they do not support multi-region distribution.

q: A designer is building a star schema for a sales data warehouse. Which of the following columns belong in the fact table rather than in a dimension table? (Choose three.)
opts: A key referencing the row in the Date dimension
why: A fact table holds the numeric measures of each event, SalesAmount and QuantitySold, plus the foreign keys that tie each row to its dimensions, such as the Date key; those keys are the near miss, because they live in the fact table even though they point at dimensions. Descriptive attributes such as product category and customer city belong in the Product and Customer dimension tables, where they are used to filter and group the facts.

q: A modern cloud analytics pipeline loads raw data directly into a powerful destination system first, and performs all transformations afterward using that destination's own compute. Which pattern is this?
why: ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the destination first and transforms it there, taking advantage of the destination's own compute power — matching the pattern described. ETL transforms data before loading it, OLTP is a transactional workload type unrelated to pipeline ordering, and a star schema is a data modeling pattern, not a load-order pattern.

q: A retailer needs to detect a spike in checkout errors within seconds of it happening, rather than discovering it in a report the next morning. Which processing approach fits?
opts: Batch processing on a nightly schedule
why: Streaming, or real-time, processing analyzes each event as it arrives, enabling detection within seconds, which fits a checkout-error spike that must be caught immediately. Batch processing, a weekly ETL job, and a monthly-refreshed OLAP cube all introduce a scheduled delay that would miss an issue happening right now.

q: A company wants one workspace where analysts query a star-schema warehouse with T-SQL on provisioned compute for steady nightly loads, data scientists run Spark notebooks over the same data lake, and engineers schedule the pipelines that feed both. Which Azure service provides all of this?
why: Synapse Analytics combines dedicated SQL pools for the warehouse, Spark pools for notebooks, and built-in pipelines for orchestration in a single workspace. Databricks covers the Spark and pipeline-like needs well but has no T-SQL dedicated warehouse pool; Data Factory orchestrates but has no query engine of its own; and SQL Managed Instance is an OLTP-oriented relational engine with neither Spark nor warehouse-scale provisioned analytics compute.

q: A team must copy data every night from fifteen sources, including SaaS applications, an on-premises SQL Server, and Blob Storage, into Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 using a visual, low-code tool, and then trigger a downstream notebook. Which service should orchestrate this?
why: Data Factory is the managed integration service with connectors for SaaS, on-premises, and Azure sources, a visual pipeline designer, scheduling triggers, and activities that can call a notebook afterward. Databricks is the near miss: it can run the notebook and even pull data in code, but it is a Spark processing platform rather than a low-code connector-driven orchestrator. Stream Analytics handles continuous event streams, not scheduled nightly copies, and Data Explorer is a query engine for telemetry.

q: A data science team needs an Apache Spark-based environment for large-scale data engineering and machine learning model training. Which Azure service fits best?
opts: An Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pool
why: Databricks is a Spark-based platform with collaborative notebooks and built-in machine learning tooling, purpose-built for this work. A Synapse dedicated SQL pool is a T-SQL data warehouse engine with no Spark runtime, so it is the near miss for anyone who equates Synapse with Spark. Stream Analytics runs SQL-like queries over event streams, and Data Factory orchestrates data movement; neither trains models or executes Spark code itself.

q: Sensor readings already flow into an Azure Event Hubs instance. The team now needs to compute a one-minute rolling average per device and raise an alert when it exceeds a threshold, using SQL-like syntax and no cluster to manage. Which service should they add?
opts: A second Azure Event Hubs namespace
An Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pool
why: Stream Analytics is the managed engine that reads from Event Hubs, applies windowed SQL-like queries such as a per-device one-minute average, and writes results or alerts to outputs. Event Hubs only ingests and buffers events, so a second namespace adds capacity but no computation. Data Factory runs scheduled batch pipelines rather than continuous queries, and a dedicated SQL pool would need the data loaded first, defeating the sub-minute requirement.

q: A company standardized on Power BI wants to add lakehouse storage, a warehouse, and data pipelines that its analysts can use from the same browser experience as their reports, as a SaaS offering with no Azure resources to deploy into a subscription. Which platform fits?
why: Fabric delivers data engineering, warehousing, pipelines, and Power BI as one SaaS tenant on OneLake, so apart from buying capacity, nothing is deployed or managed in an Azure subscription. Synapse is the near miss: it offers a similar set of workloads, but as PaaS resources that must be deployed and managed in a subscription. Databricks and Data Factory each cover only part of the picture and are likewise subscription-deployed Azure services.

q: A Power BI report needs to always reflect the very latest data in its source database at the moment a user opens it, even if query performance is slightly slower as a result. Which connectivity mode should be used?
opts: Import mode with hourly scheduled refresh
Import mode with the report pinned to a dashboard
why: DirectQuery sends each interaction to the source, so what the user sees is whatever the database holds at that moment, at the cost of slower visuals. Every Import variant copies data into Power BI's in-memory model and is only as fresh as its last refresh: hourly refresh still lags up to an hour, incremental refresh just makes each refresh cheaper, and pinning to a dashboard changes presentation, not freshness.

q: In a streaming pipeline every event is processed individually, so an aggregate such as the average reading per minute cannot be produced until the stream ends.
why: A stream has no end, which is exactly why streaming engines such as Azure Stream Analytics use temporal windows, tumbling, hopping, or sliding, to group events by time and emit an aggregate for each window as it closes. Per-minute averages, counts, and maximums are routine streaming outputs; waiting for the stream to finish is batch thinking applied to the wrong model.

q: In a star schema, the dimension tables are usually the largest tables because they hold one row for every transaction that occurred.
why: It is the fact table that holds one row per measured event, such as each sales line, so it is typically by far the largest table and the one that grows with every load. Dimension tables hold one row per product, customer, or date and are comparatively small; they supply the descriptive attributes used to filter and group the much larger set of facts.

q: Azure Data Factory keeps a copy of the data its pipelines move in its own managed data store, so a pipeline run can be replayed later from that copy.
why: Data Factory is an orchestration and movement service, not a data store; its copy activity streams data from a source to a sink such as Data Lake Storage or Azure SQL Database and retains only pipeline metadata and run logs. Re-running a pipeline reads from the source again, which is why the landing zone in the lake, not Data Factory, is where raw data should be kept for replay.

q: Azure Databricks is the only Azure service capable of running Apache Spark code, so any Spark workload must use it.
why: Spark is also available as Spark pools inside Azure Synapse Analytics, as the Data Engineering experience in Microsoft Fabric, and in Azure HDInsight. Databricks is the Spark-first platform with the richest notebook, collaboration, and machine learning tooling, which is why it is the usual answer for a dedicated data science workload, but it is a choice, not the only option.

q: Microsoft Fabric is a platform-as-a-service offering that you deploy into your own Azure subscription and virtual network, in the same way as Azure Synapse Analytics.
why: Fabric is software as a service: capacity is assigned to a tenant and workspaces are created in the browser, with nothing to deploy or manage in an Azure subscription or virtual network (a Fabric capacity can be bought through Azure, but it is a license for compute, not infrastructure you run). That is one of the main differences from Synapse, which is a PaaS workspace deployed and managed as an Azure resource. Fabric's other defining trait is OneLake, the single shared data lake under all of its workloads.

q: A team is deciding whether a single Azure Synapse Analytics workspace can replace several separate services. Which of the following capabilities are available inside the workspace? (Choose three.)
opts: A serverless SQL pool that queries files in the data lake and bills per query
A dedicated SQL pool with provisioned compute for a data warehouse
Apache Spark pools for notebooks and big-data processing
A built-in in-memory cache for sub-millisecond key lookups
why: Serverless SQL pools, dedicated SQL pools, and Spark pools, together with pipelines, are the engines that make Synapse a unified analytics workspace. An in-memory key-value cache is the near miss: that is a separate service, Azure Cache for Redis, aimed at operational applications rather than analytics, and nothing in Synapse plays that role.

q: A company needs to run fast, ad hoc analytical queries over huge volumes of time-stamped log and telemetry data, exploring it interactively without first modeling it into a star schema. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
opts: An Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pool
why: Data Explorer is optimized for interactive exploration of time-series log and telemetry data at scale using Kusto Query Language, with no up-front dimensional modeling. A dedicated SQL pool is the near miss, since it also handles large analytical volumes, but it expects data loaded into modeled warehouse tables. Stream Analytics processes events in flight rather than exploring history, and Azure SQL Database is an OLTP engine not sized for petabyte-scale log scans.

q: An operations lead wants a single screen showing a revenue tile from the Finance report and a ticket-volume tile from the Support report, which use different datasets (semantic models), for at-a-glance monitoring. Which Power BI item should be created?
why: A dashboard is a single page of tiles pinned from one or more reports, and because it pins visuals rather than binding to a model it can combine tiles from different datasets. A report is the near miss: it can have many pages, but every page is built on one dataset, so it cannot natively mix Finance and Support data. A dataset (now called a semantic model) is the model a report queries, and a dataflow is reusable Power Query preparation logic upstream of datasets.

q: A Synapse serverless SQL pool continues to accrue compute charges while idle, so it should be paused outside working hours just like a dedicated SQL pool.
why: A serverless SQL pool has no provisioned compute to pause; it bills only for the data each query processes, so an idle pool costs nothing. It is the dedicated SQL pool that reserves compute and bills continuously whether or not queries run, which is why pausing it outside working hours is a standard cost control.

q: A team is describing what Microsoft Fabric bundles into one SaaS platform. Which of the following are components of Fabric? (Choose three.)
opts: OneLake, a single shared data lake under every workload
Power BI for reporting and dashboards
Data Factory-style pipelines for data integration
Azure Cache for Redis as the platform's in-memory cache
why: OneLake, Power BI, and Data Factory-style pipelines are core Fabric experiences, alongside Data Engineering, Data Warehouse, and Data Science. Azure Cache for Redis is the wrong one: it is a separate Azure PaaS service for application caching and is not part of Fabric.
