(Fabric does now include its own SQL database and Cosmos DB items, so do not rule out databases in Fabric altogether.)

q: A company wants dashboards that update within seconds of new sales events occurring, rather than refreshing once a day. Which combination of processing approach and Azure service fits?
opts: Streaming processing using Azure Stream Analytics
Batch processing using a nightly Azure Data Factory pipeline
OLTP processing using Azure SQL Database alone
Batch processing using a weekly Power BI dataset refresh
why: Streaming processing handles events continuously as they arrive, and Stream Analytics is built for exactly this near-real-time scenario. A nightly or weekly batch job, by definition, only refreshes on its schedule, not within seconds of an event, and OLTP alone processes transactions — it doesn't provide the aggregation or dashboard refresh mechanism this scenario needs.

q: A team needs one platform where data engineers build Spark notebooks for transformation, data warehouse analysts run T-SQL against that same underlying data with no separate copy, and business users build Power BI reports — all sharing one common storage layer without duplicating data between tools. Which is the best fit?
opts: Microsoft Fabric, because its workloads share a single storage layer
Azure Data Factory, because pipelines can feed all three tools independently
Azure Databricks, because Spark notebooks can also publish Power BI reports directly
Three separate services, each keeping its own copy of the data
why: Microsoft Fabric's OneLake is a single shared data lake underneath Spark (Data Engineering), T-SQL (Data Warehouse), and Power BI experiences, so none of them needs its own duplicated copy — exactly what this scenario asks for. Data Factory alone only moves and orchestrates data, it doesn't provide Spark notebooks or a warehouse engine; Databricks doesn't natively provide a T-SQL warehouse engine or built-in Power BI reporting; and three separate services with separate copies is precisely the duplication this scenario wants to avoid.

q: A team already has a heavily modeled data warehouse in a Synapse dedicated SQL pool, but also needs to explore raw, high-volume application log data that changes shape often and hasn't been modeled into any schema yet. Which service should they add for that specific need?
opts: A second Synapse dedicated SQL pool
why: Azure Data Explorer is built specifically for exploring raw, fast-changing log and telemetry data without first modeling it into a schema, complementing rather than replacing an already-modeled Synapse warehouse. Adding a second dedicated SQL pool would just mean modeling the same raw data before it could be queried, and Azure SQL Managed Instance and Azure Files are relational and file-storage services, not built for ad hoc log-scale analytical queries at all.

q: Azure Event Hubs runs the SQL-like queries that aggregate incoming events; Azure Stream Analytics is only needed when the results must be written to a destination such as Power BI.
why: The roles are the other way round. Event Hubs is the ingestion front door that receives and buffers millions of events per second but performs no analysis. Stream Analytics is the processing engine that reads those events, runs windowed SQL-like queries over them, and writes results to outputs such as Power BI, Azure SQL Database, or a data lake.

q: A BI team wants to define one shared set of Power Query data-cleaning steps just once, so several different Power BI reports and datasets (semantic models) can all reuse the same cleaned-up data instead of repeating the same transformations in every report. Which Power BI concept fits?
why: A dataflow is a reusable set of data preparation logic built with Power Query that multiple datasets can draw from, avoiding repeated transformation work across reports. A dashboard is a page of pinned visualization tiles rather than a data preparation concept, a workspace is a container that organizes content rather than transforming data, and DirectQuery is a live-query connectivity mode, not a shared transformation layer.

q: Which of the following statements about Power BI reports and dashboards are true? (Choose three.)
opts: A report can span multiple pages of interactive visualizations built against one dataset (semantic model)
A dashboard is typically a single page of tiles pinned from one or more reports
A dashboard can display tiles sourced from more than one underlying dataset
A dashboard is authored in Power BI Desktop and then published to the Power BI service
why: A report is multi-page and bound to one dataset (now called a semantic model), while a dashboard is a single page of pinned tiles that can draw on several reports and datasets. The near miss is the claim that dashboards are authored in Power BI Desktop: it describes how reports are made. Dashboards exist only in the Power BI service, where tiles are pinned from published reports; Power BI Desktop authors reports, not dashboards.

q: A team already runs its data warehousing and Spark processing inside one Azure Synapse Analytics workspace and wants to also orchestrate data movement pipelines without standing up a separate resource just for that. Which capability lets them do this inside the same workspace?
opts: A separate Azure Data Factory instance linked to the workspace
A Spark notebook scheduled to copy the data in code
why: Synapse pipelines are the Data Factory engine built directly into the workspace, giving the same copy activities, connectors, and triggers with no additional resource. A separate Data Factory instance is the near miss: it works, but it is exactly the extra resource the team wants to avoid. A scheduled Spark notebook turns connector-driven movement into custom code to maintain, and Stream Analytics is for continuous event processing rather than scheduled pipelines.

q: A team wants to run near real-time analytical queries directly against data in an operational Azure Cosmos DB container, without building and maintaining a separate ETL pipeline to copy that data into a warehouse first. Which capability fits?
opts: A dedicated SQL pool loaded nightly
Azure Data Factory with a weekly schedule
why: Azure Synapse Link connects an operational store like Cosmos DB directly to Synapse Analytics for near real-time analytics, with no separate ETL pipeline required (for new work, mirroring into Microsoft Fabric is the recommended successor approach). A nightly-loaded dedicated SQL pool and a weekly Data Factory pipeline both introduce a scheduled delay, and Dynamic Data Masking is an Azure SQL Database security feature unrelated to analytical connectivity.

q: A pipeline built in Azure Data Factory needs to pull data from an on-premises SQL Server database that sits behind a corporate firewall with no direct path from the public internet. Which component does the pipeline need?
why: The self-hosted integration runtime is installed on a machine inside the private network and gives Data Factory a path to reach data stores that aren't accessible from the public internet, like an on-premises SQL Server behind a firewall. The Azure integration runtime only handles cloud-to-cloud movement, the Azure-SSIS integration runtime is for running lifted SSIS packages specifically, and a serverless SQL pool is a Synapse query engine, not an integration runtime at all.

q: To query Parquet files in a data lake from a Synapse dedicated SQL pool with T-SQL, the files must first be copied into warehouse tables with a bulk-load step.
why: PolyBase lets a dedicated SQL pool define an external table over files in the lake and query them in place with ordinary T-SQL, with no load step. Copying the data into internal tables is still common for the heaviest, most frequently queried data because it is faster, but it is a performance choice rather than a requirement for the query to work.

q: Which of the following are time-based window types used by Azure Stream Analytics to aggregate a continuous event stream? (Choose three.)
why: Tumbling, hopping, and sliding windows are the real time-based window types Stream Analytics uses to group and aggregate streaming events over an interval. 'Rolling window' isn't one of Stream Analytics' defined window types, even though it sounds similar.

q: Data must stay in an Amazon S3 bucket for compliance reasons, but analysts want to query it from a Fabric lakehouse without building pipelines or copying it. Which Fabric capability fits?
why: A shortcut is a live reference to external storage, including Amazon S3, that makes the data appear in the lakehouse with no movement or duplication. Mirroring replicates databases such as Azure SQL Database or Cosmos DB into OneLake, which copies data, a Dataflows Gen2 refresh moves transformed data, and an Eventstream ingests streaming events.

q: A team wants the contents of an operational Azure SQL Database to appear continuously in OneLake in near real time, in Delta format, with no pipeline authoring. Which capability does this?
why: Mirroring continuously replicates an external database into OneLake and handles change tracking automatically, with data landing in Delta format and queryable through the SQL analytics endpoint. A shortcut references external files rather than replicating a database, Lakeflow pipelines are an Azure Databricks feature, and a scheduled notebook would be custom code to maintain.

q: Business analysts who know Power Query want to build reusable, low-code transformation logic in Fabric without writing code. Which tool fits?
why: Dataflows Gen2 is the low-code, visual experience for building reusable transformation logic with Power Query. Spark notebooks are code-first, an Eventstream ingests streaming events, and the real-time hub is a catalog of streaming data rather than a transformation tool.

q: Events arrive from Azure Event Hubs and Apache Kafka. The team wants to route, filter, and transform them before landing them in a KQL database in Fabric. Which component does this?
why: Eventstream connects to streaming sources, routes, filters, and transforms events, and lands them in destinations such as a lakehouse or a KQL database. Activator triggers actions when conditions are met, a Real-Time dashboard visualizes data, and a shortcut references existing storage.

q: An operations team wants an automatic alert or action the moment streaming sensor data crosses a defined condition. Which Real-Time Intelligence component provides this?
why: Activator triggers automated actions when streaming data meets conditions you define. An Eventhouse stores and queries time-series data with KQL, Power BI Q&A answers typed questions with charts, and Dataflows Gen2 prepares data with Power Query.

q: A team needs a Fabric store for high-volume time-series telemetry that engineers can explore with Kusto Query Language. Which item fits?
opts: An Eventhouse with a KQL database
why: An Eventhouse is the database optimized for time-series and event data, queried with KQL. A warehouse is a T-SQL relational store for structured analytics, a semantic model is a reporting layer, and a shortcut is a reference to data stored elsewhere.

q: A team already runs Spark in Azure Databricks and now wants to process live event data using the same skills, treating the stream as a table that keeps growing. Which option fits?
opts: A weekly Azure Data Factory copy job
why: Spark Structured Streaming is the Spark library for streaming: read the source into a dataframe, run a query such as a count per minute, and write to a sink. A weekly copy job is batch, Import mode is a Power BI storage mode, and Azure Files is file storage.

q: An organization needs a service similar to Azure Event Hubs for ingesting events, but optimized for managing event data from Internet-of-things devices. Which service fits?
why: IoT Hub is a data ingestion service similar to Event Hubs but optimized to manage event data from IoT devices. Stream Analytics processes streams rather than ingesting from devices, Data Lake Storage Gen2 stores data, and Data Factory orchestrates pipelines.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the scope of data in batch and stream processing?
opts: Stream processing always has access to the full history of the dataset, while batch processing sees only the last 30 seconds
Batch processing can work on all the data in the dataset, while stream processing typically sees only the most recent data or a rolling time window
Both always process the same amount of data and differ only in the programming language used
Batch processing is used for simple rolling averages, while streaming is used for the most complex analytics
why: Batch processing can analyze everything in the dataset, usually with latency of hours and for complex analytics, while streaming handles individual records or micro-batches within a rolling window with latency of seconds or less, typically for simple aggregates. The other statements reverse or blur those roles.

q: Which architecture removes the separate batch layer by treating all data as a continuous stream and replaying it when historical reprocessing is needed?
why: Kappa architecture is a simpler alternative to lambda that treats everything as a stream and replays it when needed, which platforms such as Microsoft Fabric and Apache Kafka make more practical. Lambda keeps both a batch layer and a stream layer, a star schema is a warehouse modeling pattern, and medallion organizes lake zones into bronze, silver, and gold.

q: In Azure Databricks, which capability provides a unified governance layer with fine-grained access control, lineage, and discovery across data and AI assets?
why: Unity Catalog is the governance layer for data and AI assets in the workspace. Genie is the natural-language conversational interface, notebooks are collaborative coding documents, and Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines is a framework for building incremental pipelines.

q: A team wants to declare what its output tables should contain and let Azure Databricks handle execution order, dependency tracking, and incremental processing for a continuously running ingestion pipeline. Which framework fits?
why: Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines is a declarative framework: you define the outputs and Databricks manages ordering, dependencies, and incremental processing, and it is recommended for production ingestion. Notebooks are imperative code, Genie is a natural-language query interface, and Unity Catalog governs data rather than building pipelines.

q: Business users want to type questions such as 'what were sales by region last quarter' in plain English and have Azure Databricks generate and run the SQL against Delta Lake data. Which feature provides this?
why: Genie is the conversational natural-language interface that generates and runs SQL over Delta Lake data. Unity Catalog governs access and lineage, a Databricks SQL warehouse is the engine that executes queries, and Lakeflow pipelines build data pipelines.

q: A Power BI semantic model should read Delta tables in OneLake directly, with in-memory-style speed and without importing data or scheduling refreshes. Which storage mode does this?
why: Direct Lake reads Delta tables from OneLake directly, combining in-memory-style speed with the scale of a data lake and no separate import or refresh cycle. Import copies data into the model and needs scheduled refreshes, DirectQuery sends live queries to the source on each interaction, and a dataflow refresh prepares data upstream.

q: In a data model, a Product dimension table relates to a separate Category table that holds more detail about each category. What is this design called?
why: When dimension tables relate further to additional detail tables, the design is a snowflake schema. A star schema has fact tables relating directly to dimension tables only. A flat file and a key-value store are not relational modeling patterns of this kind.

q: Which term names the tabular analytical model, which defines measures, relationships, and hierarchies and is built from related tables, that has replaced older cubes as the preferred approach in Power BI and Fabric?
why: A semantic model, formerly called a dataset, defines the measures, dimensions, relationships, and hierarchies that reports are built on. A dataflow is reusable data preparation logic, the SQL analytics endpoint is a T-SQL access point to lakehouse tables, and the real-time hub is a catalog of streaming data.

q: An analyst wants a Power BI visual that identifies which factors most strongly drive a selected metric, such as customer churn. Which visual fits?
why: The key influencers visual shows which factors most strongly drive a selected metric. A decomposition tree supports interactive drill-down across dimensions to see what contributes to a value, a smart narrative writes a text summary, and a card shows a single number.

q: A team has semi-structured files and runs Spark notebooks for data science, but analysts also want to query the same Delta tables with T-SQL without starting a Spark session. Which Fabric item fits best?
opts: A Power BI dashboard pinned from several reports
A Fabric lakehouse, which automatically creates a SQL analytics endpoint
A Power BI Desktop file with imported tables
An Eventstream that routes incoming events
why: A Fabric lakehouse stores Delta tables in OneLake, works well with Spark and mixed or semi-structured data, and automatically creates a SQL analytics endpoint for T-SQL queries. A dashboard, a Desktop file, and an Eventstream do not store and expose Delta tables.

q: Creating a OneLake shortcut to an Amazon S3 bucket copies the bucket's data into OneLake.
why: A shortcut is a live reference: the data appears as if it were in the lakehouse but is not copied or duplicated, and no pipeline is needed. Copying data requires pipelines, dataflows, or notebooks, and mirroring replicates databases.

q: Fabric mirroring requires you to build and schedule a data pipeline to copy changes from the source database.
why: Mirroring replicates an external database into OneLake in near real time and handles change tracking automatically; you configure the source connection once and no pipeline authoring is needed.

q: The same Delta table can serve as a streaming sink, with data written to it in real time, and as a source for batch queries.
why: That is one of the key benefits of Delta Lake: unified batch and streaming on one table, so separate storage for historical and live data is not needed. Reliability and schema enforcement come along with it.

q: Azure Event Hubs guarantees exactly-once delivery of every event.
why: Event Hubs delivers events within a partition in order and guarantees at-least-once delivery, so a consumer can see the same event more than once and downstream processing has to tolerate duplicates.

q: Which of the following are components of Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric? (Choose four.)
opts: Eventstreams for ingesting, routing, and transforming streaming data
Activator for triggering actions on conditions
Dedicated SQL pools in Azure Synapse Analytics
why: Real-Time Intelligence combines Eventstreams, an Eventhouse, Real-Time dashboards, and Activator, with the real-time hub as a catalog. Dedicated SQL pools belong to Azure Synapse Analytics rather than being part of Fabric's Real-Time Intelligence.

q: Which of the following are ways to bring data into OneLake in Microsoft Fabric? (Choose four.)
opts: Pinning a dashboard tile in Power BI
why: Pipelines, shortcuts, mirroring, and Eventstream are the ingestion paths described for Fabric, covering pipeline ETL, zero-copy federation, near-real-time replication, and streaming. Pinning a dashboard tile is a way of arranging visuals, not of ingesting data.

q: Which three are components of Azure Databricks? (Choose three.)
why: Unity Catalog, Databricks SQL, and Genie are among the core Databricks components. OneLake is the unified data lake of Microsoft Fabric, and a dedicated SQL pool is a provisioned warehouse engine in Azure Synapse Analytics.
